title: A cart, a bouquet, an ordinary errand.

title: Wicked Whoopies: a little stop with a very large whoopie pie.
summary: A family visit to Wicked Whoopies in Freeport, Maine: James, giant whoopie-pie displays, a colorful shop and useful sensory and access planning notes.
search: Freeport, Maine · From the family album Wicked Whoopies: a little stop with a very large whoopie pie. Orange walls, turquoise chairs, and a stack of whoopie pies taller than James. A Maine treat stop with a sense of humor. October 16, 2026 · A family visit The full-size James and the considerably oversized whoopie pies. From our family camera roll. A shop with a tower of whoopie pies has made its intentions quite clear. We are here for something sweet, and nobody is taking the décor too seriously. Our visit to Wicked Whoopies in Freeport, Maine, gave us exactly the sort of photographs I love keeping: James in his pink shirt, a wrapped treat in hand, standing beside a display that is delightfully out of proportion. The room is full of color. Orange walls, purple shelving, turquoise tables and chairs, blue flowers, and enormous red letters spelling “SMILE.” It is cheerful, a little theatrical, and thoroughly committed to its subject. A whoopie pie apparently deserves a pedestal. Several, in fact. James wore his hearing protection, as you can see in the photographs. That belongs in the family album just as much as the treat and the pink shirt. The pictures also give another family a useful preview of the bright interior before deciding whether it looks like their kind of stop. Plenty of color, right down to the shelving. This wider view is useful if you like to see a place before arriving. What makes this worth considering is its scale as an outing. You can build a small plan around a treat shop without needing a whole afternoon of activities. A browse, a choice, a photograph if everyone wants one, and then on with the day. My favorite detail is the contrast between the whoopie pie in James’s hand and the enormous versions behind him. One for the road; several that would require a moving van. Keep the plan small. Show the shop photographs beforehand if a preview helps. Bring the hearing protection or communication supports your family usually uses. If a particular flavor matters, call before making the trip: the shop’s selection can differ from the online store. There were tables and chairs in the shop when these photos were taken. You can ask about seating when you call, or plan to take your purchase with you. A short visit is a perfectly reasonable plan. A smaller stack, and another picture worth keeping. The useful details. Sound and light: Expect a visually busy setting: saturated colors, oversized displays and bright overhead lighting. The photographs cannot tell us how loud the shop will be during your visit. Ask the shop about quieter times if that would help. Mobility and facilities: Our photos show indoor seating and the shop floor, but do not establish step-free entry, doorway clearance, accessible parking or restroom facilities. Call the store about the specific route and facilities you need. Food: Wicked Whoopies’ current FAQ says it does not offer gluten-free or vegan whoopie pies. Check ingredients and any allergy or cross-contact questions directly before buying. Read the shop’s FAQ ↗ Put it in the address book. title: A camping swing, very much at home.
summary: Our portable Walmart swing, Yankee frugality, and autism-and-camping planning: familiar comforts, communication and room for a shorter trip. Original family photo.
search: Portable for camping · A little Yankee frugalityA camping swing, very much at home.Made for the campsite. Claimed by the stuffed animals. Our portable Walmart camping swing has earned its place at home, too—with a few thoughts on autism, camping, and bringing familiar comforts along.October 21, 2026 · From the family notebookOur Walmart camping swing, already full of stuffed animals, just after we moved in. Excuse the older photograph from just after we moved in, but this is one of those finds worth showing before the room is ready for its close-up. We love this swing. The stuffed animals seem fairly committed to it, too. It came from Walmart, and it was made for camping: an Ozark Trail hammock-style chair with its own folding frame. Not an elaborate installation. Not something that needed a dedicated room. Just a portable chair that turned out to be a very welcome part of our home. A little Yankee frugality. Yes, from Walmart.Our version of Yankee frugality is not about making life smaller. It is about getting good use out of what we bring into it. Does it work? Will we actually use it? Do we already own something that does the job?Something does not become less useful because it came from Walmart, or more useful because it came from a specialty catalog. A good find is a good find. We can appreciate a lovely old quilt and a practical camping chair in the same room. Neither needs to apologize for the other.Nor is thrift simply a contest to pay the least. The bargain that sits unused is not much of a bargain. A chair made for camping that also becomes a favorite at home has a rather better argument for its place.That is the appeal here: not buying a whole new room, not replacing something because it is no longer new, and not confusing an impressive label with a useful object. Just noticing what works for your family and continuing to enjoy it. The price tag is not the point. The life you get out of a thing is. Find it at Walmart.Check the blue Ozark Trail hammock-chair listing ↗Availability note, October 21, 2026: The blue listing showed shipping, pickup and delivery unavailable when checked. It remains useful for identifying the chair and reading reviews, but it is not a promise that you can order it today.Browse Walmart’s current hammock-chair listings ↗. Other designs are not the chair in our photograph and have not been tested by our family.These are ordinary, non-affiliate shopping links. Our photograph shows an earlier purchase, not a guarantee of an identical production version. Compare the exact model, seller, instructions, price and availability before ordering. The portable part is the point.This is camping furniture, and that is part of its appeal. Walmart’s description for this model lists a folding frame and an included carry bag for transport and storage. The chair can come along with the camping gear instead of being a permanent fixture.That is worth knowing whether your interest is campsite seating or a chair you can put away when you need the space. Our own photograph and firsthand story are from home; this is not a campsite field test.Other owners have plenty to say, too. On October 21, 2026, Walmart’s listing showed 4.3 out of 5 stars from 466 ratings. Positive reviews describe easy setup and comfort; not every owner agrees about the fit. Read the critical reviews as well as the enthusiastic ones. That is the retailer’s listing score, not our own testing score, and it can change. A favorite does not need a specialty label.At our house, the cozy, swing-style seat found a place among James’s favorite stuffed animals. We pay attention to what he actually enjoys, not only what a product label says it is supposed to do.Sometimes the useful things are specialized. Sometimes they are in the camping aisle. We are glad we found this one. A seat full of stuffed animals is not a showroom photograph, but it is a fairly good picture of something having found its place. Autism and camping: bring a little familiar with you. A change of scenery does not have to mean changing every familiar thing. That is the camping connection this chair makes us think about: a comfortable place someone already enjoys might be something to bring along, when it suits both the person and the setting. Start with the autistic person, not an “autism-friendly” shopping list. A child, teenager or adult might enjoy a moving seat, prefer a firm, still chair, or choose something else entirely. Their preferences come first. Our chair is a home favorite; the suggestions here are for planning, not an account of taking it camping. Try the smaller version. Explore the equipment at home, or consider a short outdoor visit before committing to an overnight. Sitting outside together can be the whole plan. Nobody has to graduate to a tent. Preview the everyday details. Look at campsite photographs and maps together. Ask about bathrooms, paths, lighting, neighboring sites and noise. Plan around the person’s actual access and sensory needs, rather than assuming outdoors always means quiet. Bring what already works. Familiar food, bedding or a preferred comfort item may be worth the packing space. Keep the person’s usual communication available, including AAC—augmentative and alternative communication—where used. Plan charging, weather protection and a familiar backup; a “screen-free” trip must not mean losing a way to communicate. Keep choices real. Leave time for pauses and a quieter place to go. Respect “no,” “break” and “all done,” however they are communicated. A shorter visit or going home is an option, not a failed outing. For a person who needs substantial support, include personal care, overnight support and an individual safety plan in the arrangements. Plan for water, roads, fire, weather and emergencies; do not assume mobile service will be available. A familiar chair cannot replace those supports. And there is our Yankee-frugality point again: begin with the person’s familiar things, not a new cartful of “sensory camping essentials.” Planning references, checked October 21, 2026: National Autistic Society: holiday planning for autistic people and families, and National Park Service: before a camping trip. These are general planning resources, not endorsements of this chair. For something you can adapt to your own day, try our visual visit planner or AAC-friendly outing note. A few details before you settle in.Check the instructions, assembly, weight limit and intended movement for the exact chair you buy. Use a level, clear space and keep loose cords away from the frame and entry path; our moving-in photograph is a family snapshot, not a recommended setup. A camping chair is not automatically a therapeutic swing or suitable for every person. Follow the manufacturer’s guidance and provide the support or supervision the person needs.Product sources checked October 21, 2026: Walmart’s blue chair listing and customer ratings, and Walmart Business’s description of the same model for its folding frame and carry bag. Listings, ratings and availability can change.Disclosure: This is our family experience, not a claim of therapeutic benefit. The Walmart links are non-affiliate editorial links. title: A Love Letter to Buying Nothing
summary: A framed Boston alphabet from a local Buy Nothing group, Yankee thrift, and the art of neighborly generosity. Plus a searchable New England sharing and swap shed directory.
search: A family note · October 2026A Love Letter to Buying NothingOn Yankee thrift, the kindness of neighbors, and the beautiful things we pass along.An AUsome Life · New EnglandA framed print, a local Buy Nothing group, and a very good reminder that free need not mean ordinary.Our Boston alphabet print, shared by a neighbor through a local Buy Nothing group. Family photograph; the artwork bears a Mr. Boddington credit. The latest addition to our home came already framed: a Boston alphabet, from Frog Pond to the Zakim Bridge, surrounded by a generous green mat and a white frame that has plainly seen some life. Which, really, is part of the point.We found it through our local Buy Nothing group. Someone had something worth enjoying and offered it to a neighbor. We happened to be the neighbors who brought it home.It's not just the sort of thing I would happily admire in a shop. It's the sort of thing that makes a room feel like the people who live there actually live there. A little Boston, letter by letter.There is a joke tucked into nearly every square. A is for Arabesque on Frog Pond—which sent us straight back to our own Boston Common Frog Pond guide. F is for Fall at Faneuil Hall. There is the Green Monster, Make Way for the Ducklings, and the Red Line. Newbury Street gets the caption “Not Cheap,” which is a good joke for a picture that came home free.That this print came to us through a neighbor makes us treasure it all the more.To me, that's good Yankee frugality. Not refusing to enjoy beautiful things. Not turning household life into a competition to spend the least. It's appreciating what's already here, knowing the difference between price and value, and being delighted when a useful or lovely thing finds the right person. The best things in a home are not always the things we went shopping for. The joy of receiving matters, too.We talk about the pleasure of giving, and rightly so. But Buy Nothing communities ask us to be comfortable on both sides of the exchange.One week, perhaps you are the person with a lamp to spare. Another week, you are the person who could really use one. A borrowed folding table, a box of books, an extra frame, a garden tool you only need twice: these things don't have to sit in a cupboard waiting to be useful someday.And neither does kindness have to be a grand gesture. It can be a simple message, a good photograph of the item, a cheerful pickup, and an uncomplicated thank-you.There's dignity in being able to ask. And there's something heartening about a community where a person who receives today is never expected to justify their need or become a charity project. Because ordinary life has an extraordinary bill.Most families know the arithmetic of daily life: groceries, housing, school supplies, the car, the utility bill that arrived at an especially inconvenient moment. For many disabled people and families caring for disabled relatives, there can be another layer—medical bills, therapy, adaptive equipment, transportation, appointments, and the work hours that become difficult to keep.A free household item will not fix those larger pressures. Nor should neighborly generosity be used as an excuse for systems that fail to provide people with what they need. But it can ease one small expense, save one trip, or simply make an ordinary Tuesday a little nicer.And everyone belongs in these groups—not only people who are struggling financially. When households with different resources all give and receive freely, the exchange becomes a way of living together rather than a label about who needs help.It can mean choosing a beautiful framed print while keeping money for a medical bill, a family outing, the occasional good meal, or whatever makes a particular household's life work. No one should have to choose between necessity and every bit of everyday pleasure. A rather good version of the American life.We often talk about the good American life as something we acquire: the right house, the right furnishings, the right things inside it. I think there's another version worth holding on to. It's a home that feels welcoming, enough time with the people you love, a little freedom from waste and worry, and neighbors who remember that we need one another.It feels very New England to me, with the practical affection for old things, shared tools, and a sturdy frame. But the idea belongs everywhere. Every town could use a few more people willing to pass something along.There is a conservation story here, too. Reuse is not quite the same as recycling: it means keeping a perfectly serviceable thing in use rather than processing its materials. Connecticut’s Department of Energy and Environmental Protection explains the distinction. One picture changing walls will not save the planet, but it belongs to a habit that keeps good things in circulation.So here is to the generous neighbor, the well-used swap shed, the free book left for the next reader, and the perfectly good thing that doesn't need another trip to the store.And here's to our Boston alphabet, a lovely little reminder that value and price were never synonyms in the first place.The letter is personal; the guide below is practical. You'll find verified links to free-sharing groups and town reuse programs throughout New England. Worth saving · worth sharingYour Guide to Yankee FrugalityNot a prescription to do without. A handful of generous, useful habits for enjoying what we already have—and leaving a little more room for what matters. 01Ask your neighbors first.Before buying the extra tray, picture frame, bookshelf or garden tool, see whether someone nearby has one they're happy to give. A polite ask can save money and start a conversation.02Offer it while it is still good.A clean, complete, working item is a gift. Mention its condition honestly, including any flaws. Nobody needs a mystery repair project unless they want one.03Find the town swap shed.Many New England towns have reuse sheds or swap shops at recycling centers. Some are volunteer-run or seasonal, and many require a resident sticker. Always check first.04Borrow the once-a-year thing.Ask your library about a Library of Things; try borrowing the telescope, sewing machine, power tool, or board game before buying one to store for years.05Make pickup easy for real people.Give clear directions, communicate about timing, and consider transportation and accessibility needs. A free item loses its charm if collecting it becomes an obstacle course.06Receive without apology.People share because they want the item used. You don't have to explain your finances. A genuine thank-you—and passing on something else when you can—is enough. title: We like a good day. We also like knowing where the bathroom is.
summary: About An AUsome Life, a long-running New England family account focused on autism-inclusive life, practical access and useful recommendations.
search: Meet usWe like a good day. We also like knowing where the bathroom is.An AUsome Life is about the life we actually live: New England outings, clothes worth wearing again, hotels that work as home base, food people will eat, useful things that earn their space, and profound autism as one real part of the family story.No tragedy framing. No inspirational confetti. No pretending logistics do not exist.New EnglandClassic styleFamily travelUseful thingsOlder-teen access Wells Beach · family camera roll.One scoop in Lexington.The Book Barn, Niantic.A good life is allowed to be practical.Sometimes the difference between a lovely afternoon and an early exit is not profound. It is parking, a warm pool, the right food, a quieter corner, or having the charger you thought was in the bag. We write those things down.Our family includes an older autistic teen with very high support needs. We use profound autism for that experience. It tells you something important about support. It does not tell you the whole person.That perspective changes what we notice: the warm pool, the easier closure, the quiet place to pause, the product that removes a step, the restaurant that makes an ordinary dinner possible. These are one family's field notes, not a universal rulebook.High support needs can be profound. So can taste, humor, annoyance, adolescence and joy.Our language standardProfoundly Awesome Classic, not costumeWe like prep and New England style. We do not need every room to look as though a lobster trap has been promoted to furniture.Useful, not cleverIf the organizer needs its own organizing system, we have probably created a second problem.Age-respectful alwaysHigh support needs do not erase adolescence, personal style or dignity.Tell me the thingIs the pool warm? Does the zipper cooperate? Is there a surprise subscription? Put that near the top.

This is the standard we use when researching calendar events, Favorite Places and practical guides. We look for current official information first, then use public visitor reports as a secondary reality check when they add useful lived detail. We label uncertainty instead of turning it into a promise. What we checkEight questions before “accessible.”Not every venue publishes every answer. An honest “not confirmed” is more useful than a confident guess. Wheelchair + adaptive strollerStep-free entrances, ramps, elevators, doorway routes, seating, transfer points, wheelchair or mobility-device rentals and whether the route actually works beyond the lobby. Terrain + distancePavement, packed gravel, loose gravel, grass, roots, slopes, long walks, mud, snow and places where a wheeled mobility device may need more help than a general accessibility label suggests. Sensory + communicationNoise, lighting, crowd density, smells, startling effects, quiet spaces, sensory kits, visual supports, AAC-friendly participation, flexible movement, re-entry and whether “sensory-friendly” changes the environment or only the schedule. Blind + low-vision accessBraille, large print, tactile or verbal description, audio description, contrast, wayfinding and lighting changes. We avoid assuming that a wheelchair-accessible route is also an accessible visual experience. Deaf + hard-of-hearing accessCaptions, ASL interpretation, assistive-listening systems, visual announcements, hearing loops/headsets and how far in advance an accommodation must be requested. Restrooms + practical careAccessible and family restrooms, changing tables, and an adult-size or height-adjustable changing table only when a venue specifically publishes that information. We never imply that a particular family uses a facility simply because we report that it exists. Parking + arrivalAccessible spaces, drop-off, distance to the entrance, the best door to use, city parking realities, whether a shuttle runs and what happens after dark. Weather + escape planOutdoor exposure, snow, ice, rain, heat, muddy paths, low light, indoor backup options, break spaces and how easy it is to shorten the visit or leave. Evidence labels How strong is the information? Organizer-confirmedA current event page, ticket page, venue policy or direct accessibility statement. This is our starting point. Venue access guideA current accessibility, visitor, trail, seating or building guide that adds detail beyond the event listing. Public visitor reportA review or public Q&A can reveal practical realities—steepness, crowd bottlenecks, muddy ground, stroller frustration—but it is anecdotal and dated. We label it as such and do not let it override newer official information. Not confirmedWe looked and did not find a reliable current answer. That is a prompt to contact the venue, not permission to guess. We do not convert “ADA accessible” into a blanket promise about the whole experience. We do not assume a venue has an adult-size changing table, sensory room, ASL interpreter, elevator or smooth terrain unless we can confirm it. We do not present a visitor review as a verified current venue policy. We date access research because buildings, programs, construction, staffing and weather conditions change. We do not diagnose what a person “should” need. The information is there so each reader can decide what matters for their own visit. The website itself Access should apply here, too. We aim for readable type, strong contrast, keyboard-accessible navigation, useful headings, meaningful link text, alt text for informative images, layouts that work on smaller screens, and controls that do not rely on color alone. Visual planners are editable because one person’s helpful wording or picture can be another person’s clutter. Our tools use visible words alongside icons, large controls, familiar examples, keyboard access and clear optional sections. Preselected settings make it possible to finish without adjusting every detail. Color choices always have written names; color alone does not carry an instruction. Our creative standardBeautiful, useful, respectful.Our default look is preppy New England: Nantucket light, Vermont warmth, recognizable objects and natural materials. Communication pictures keep a clear subject and a familiar word. Decoration belongs around the task, where it can add pleasure without obscuring meaning.We create and publish lawful, family-friendly content. Sexual content, graphic violence, hate imagery, exploitation, harassment and deceptive images of real people have no place here. We respect privacy, consent, intellectual property and the dignity of the people we portray. AI-created illustrations are identified as such and are never presented as family photographs or evidence about a real venue.The picture-card studio currently offers a reviewed starter collection and private, in-tab photo selection. It has no public upload gallery and does not generate new images live. Personal photos are not sent to us or automatically inspected. Use only appropriate pictures you are permitted to use. Any future live image-generation service must include input and output moderation before it is made available. If a page is difficult to use—or a field note is wrong, stale or missing—please contact us with the page and the detail that needs attention.
